title: Fact Sheet: Opening New York City’s Closed Primary System
plain_title: The case for opening city primaries to independent voters
what_they_audited: A one-page fact sheet from Citizens Union laying out the organization's case for opening New York City's primary elections to voters who are not registered with a political party.
background: Under current rules, only voters registered with a political party can vote in New York City's primary elections.

findings.plain: More than a million New Yorkers who are not registered with a party cannot vote in city primaries, and the fact sheet describes them as the fastest-growing part of the electorate.
findings.quote: Over 1 million “independents” are excluded from voting in the NYC primary

findings.plain: Voters without a party affiliation in the city skew young, and most are voters of color.
findings.quote: Nearly half of unaffiliated voters in NYC are under 40.

findings.plain: The fact sheet says these voters want to take part, and that being shut out of primaries makes them less likely to vote later in the year.
findings.quote: When excluded from primaries, they’re less likely to vote in general elections.

findings.plain: Because turnout in party primaries is low, the fact sheet says a small slice of the electorate effectively picks the mayor.
findings.quote: In low turnout primaries, mayors are effectively chosen by fewer than 10% of electorate.

findings.plain: Citizens Union says New York City is unusual among American cities in keeping a closed primary, and points to open or nonpartisan primaries in Los Angeles, Boston and Chicago.
findings.quote: New York City is an outlier – nearly all U.S. cities use a version of open primaries.

findings.plain: The fact sheet cites a review by former U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch concluding that open primaries would not reduce any protected class's ability to take part in the political process.
findings.quote: there is no basis for finding that [open primaries] would in any way diminish the ability of any protected class to participate in the political process.

recommendations: Open New York City's primary elections to voters who are not registered with a political party, with candidates still appearing under their party affiliation and still able to seek support from party organizations.
